• Fungi are not classified as omnivores; they are primarily decomposers that break down organic matter.
 
• Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, play a crucial role in nutrient cycling by breaking down dead organisms.
 
• Herbivores, also known as primary consumers, feed exclusively on plant material.
 
• Carnivores, which can be secondary or tertiary consumers, feed on other animals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trophic Levels:**

 
 
• The position an organism occupies in a food chain, which includes primary producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, and decomposers.
 
• Primary producers, like plants, convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **Food Chain:**
 
 
• A linear sequence of organisms where each is fed upon by the next member in the chain.
 
 
 
• **Food Web:**
 
 
• A complex network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, demonstrating how different organisms are interdependent.
 
 
 
• **Decomposers:**
 
 
• Organisms like bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter, returning essential nutrients to the ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Energy Transfer:**
 
 
• In ecosystems, energy flows from primary producers through various consumer levels, with significant energy loss at each trophic level due to metabolic processes.

subject: GK
question: Choose the INCORRECT statement about lichens.

options.text: Lichens are seen slow-growing large coloured patches on the bark of trees.
Fungi are found in lichen living a symbiotic life.
Fungi and cyanobacteria both lives in lichens independently.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lichens are a symbiotic association between fungi and a photosynthetic partner, typically algae or cyanobacteria.
 
• The fungal component, known as the mycobiont, provides structure and protection while the photosynthetic partner, known as the photobiont, produces food through photosynthesis.
 
• Fungi and cyanobacteria do not live independently within lichens; they form a mutualistic relationship where both partners benefit.
 
• Lichens grow slowly and can form large, colored patches on surfaces like tree bark, rocks, and soil.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Symbiosis**

 
 
• Symbiosis is an interaction between two different organisms living in close physical association, typically to the advantage of both.
 
• In lichens, the symbiotic relationship is between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium.
 
 
 
• **Types of Lichens**
 
 
• Crustose: Crust-like lichens that adhere tightly to the substrate.
 
• Foliose: Leafy lichens that have a flat, leaf-like structure.
 
• Fruticose: Shrubby or hair-like lichens with a complex, branching structure.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Importance**
 
 
• Lichens play a vital role in soil formation by breaking down rocks into soil particles.
 
• They are bioindicators of air quality, as they are sensitive to air pollution and environmental changes.
 
 
 
• **Lichen Reproduction**
 
 
• Lichens can reproduce asexually through fragmentation, where pieces of the lichen break off and grow into new individuals.
 
• They can also reproduce sexually via fungal spores, which must encounter a compatible photosynthetic partner to form a new lichen.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Frogs have four-chambered heart**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Frogs have a three-chambered heart**, consisting of two atria and one ventricle.
 
• The three-chambered heart in amphibians like frogs allows for partial mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
 
• This structure is efficient for their dual life in water and on land, where they can absorb oxygen through their skin.
 
• Unlike frogs, birds and mammals possess a more complex four-chambered heart, which completely separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Heart Chambers in Vertebrates**

 
 
• **Fish:** Two-chambered heart (one atrium and one ventricle)
 
• **Amphibians:** Three-chambered heart (two atria and one ventricle)
 
• **Reptiles:** Typically three-chambered heart, except for crocodiles which have four chambers
 
• **Birds and Mammals:** Four-chambered heart (two atria and two ventricles)
 
 
 
• **Functions of Heart Chambers**
 
 
• Atria receive blood from the body and lungs.
 
• Ventricles pump blood out to the body and lungs.
 
• A four-chambered heart allows for complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is more efficient for high-energy demands.
 
 
 
• **Circulatory Systems**
 
 
• **Single Circulatory System:** Found in fish, blood passes through the heart once during each complete circuit.
 
• **Double Circulatory System:** Found in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, blood passes through the heart twice, providing more efficient oxygenation.
 
 
 
• **Adaptive Significance**
 
 
• A four-chambered heart supports endothermy (warm-bloodedness) in birds and mammals.
 
• Efficient circulation is crucial for sustaining high metabolic rates and activity levels.

• Sponges (Phylum Porifera) are characterized by the presence of a **water canal system**, which facilitates water circulation for feeding, respiration, and excretion.
 
• **Choanocytes**, or collar cells, are specialized cells in sponges responsible for creating water currents and trapping food particles.
 
• The water canal system includes structures such as **ostia (pores), spongocoel (central cavity), and osculum (exit opening)**, ensuring efficient water flow.
 
• Sponges lack tissues and organs but have a unique cellular organization that supports their **filter-feeding mechanism**.
 
• They exhibit **asymmetry or radial symmetry**, making them distinct from other animal phyla.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Choanocytes are essential for the sponge's filter-feeding and water circulation.
 
 
 
• **Water Canal System:**
 
 
• It consists of pathways like ostia, spongocoel, and osculum through which water flows.
 
• The system aids in nutrient absorption, gas exchange, and waste removal.
 
 
 
• **Skeleton of Sponges:**
 
 
• Sponges possess a skeleton made of **spicules (calcium carbonate or silica) or spongin fibers**.
 
• These structures provide support and protection.
 
 
 
• **Reproduction in Sponges:**

• **Ecological Importance:**
 
 
• Sponges play a crucial role in marine ecosystems as filter feeders, cleaning water and recycling nutrients.
 
• They also serve as habitats for various microorganisms and small marine organisms.

question: Which type of placentation is characterized by the ovules developing on the inner wall of the ovary or on peripheral part, as seen in mustard and argemone?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Parietal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Parietal placentation occurs when the ovules are attached to the inner walls of the ovary or on its peripheral part.
 
• This type of placentation is commonly observed in plants like **mustard** (Brassica) and **argemone**.
 
• The ovary in parietal placentation is typically unilocular but may become bilocular or multilocular due to the development of a false septum.
 
• In this arrangement, the ovules are borne on the ovary walls rather than on a central column.
 
• Parietal placentation is distinct from other types such as axile, basal, or free central, each of which has a unique ovule arrangement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Placentation**: It refers to the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. It plays a key role in plant reproduction and is an important taxonomic characteristic.
 
• **Axile placentation**: The ovules are attached to a central axis in a multilocular ovary, as seen in plants like tomato and lemon.
 
• **Basal placentation**: The ovules are borne at the base of the ovary, as in marigold and sunflower.
 
• **Free central placentation**: The ovules are attached to a central column, and the ovary is unilocular, as seen in dianthus.
 
• Understanding placentation types helps in the identification and classification of flowering plants, contributing to botany and plant systematics.

question: In the context of respiration, the stage known as glycolysis involves the breaking down of _______ to pyruvic acid.
solution:
The correct answer is __glucose.__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** breakdown of glucose** into **pyruvate** within a **cell's cytoplasm** is known as** glycolysis.**
 
• During** aerobic conditions**, **pyruvate** can **diffuse into mitochondria** where it **joins the citric acid cycle** and produces **reducing equivalents** in the form of **NADH and FADH2.**
 
• The **electron transport chain** then receives these reducing equivalents, which results in the creation of **32 ATP per molecule of glucose.**
 
• Because the electron transport chain r**equires oxygen as the final electron accepto**r, **inadequate tissue oxygenation inhibits** the process of **oxidative phosphorylation.**
 
• Under **anaerobic conditions,** pyruvate has a **different fate.**
 
• Instead of **entering mitochondria**, the **cytosolic enzyme lactate dehydrogenas**e converts **pyruvate to lactate.**
 
• The **regeneration of NAD+ from NADH** is also made possible by this process.
 
• An o**xidizing cofactor called NAD+** is required to keep the **flow of glucose** through glycolysis going.
 
• **Glycolysis** produces **2 ATP per glucose molecule, **and thus provides a **direct means of producing energy **in the** absence of oxygen.**
 
• This process of **breaking down glucose in the absence of oxygen** is aptly named **anaerobic glycolysis.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lactic acid:**

 
 
• Lactic acid is mainly produced in **muscle cells and red blood cells.**
 
• It forms when the **body breaks down carbohydrates** to use for** energy** when **oxygen levels are low. **
 
 
 
• **Fructose:**
 
 
• Fructose is a type of sugar known as a** monosaccharide.**
 
 
 
• **Citric acid:**
 
 
• Citric acid is a** weak acid **that is found **naturally in all citrus fruits.**

question: _______ is an environment friendly and useful method of conversion of rural and urban organic waste into good quality manure.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Vermicomposting**__.

• **Vermicomposting** is the scientific method of making compost in which the earthworms convert the organic waste into manure rich in high nutritional content.
 
• Earthworms preys on the organic waste materials and give out “vermicasts” which are rich in nitrates and minerals such as phosphorus, magnesium, calcium and potassium.
 
• These are used as fertilizers and it enhances soil quality.
 
• **Advantages of Vermicomposting:**
 
 
• It develops roots of the plants.
 
• Highly improves the body of the soil.
 
• Vermicomposting increases the fertility and water-resistance properties of the soil.
 
• Helps in the germination, plant growth, and crop yield.
 
• Nourish soil with plant growth hormones like auxins, gibberellic acid, etc.
 
 
 
• **Disadvantages of Vermicomposting:**
 
 
• It is a long and time-consuming process and takes almost six months to convert the organic matter into usable forms.
 
• It releases a very foul odour.
 
• Vermicomposting requires high maintenance. The feed should be added periodically and care should be taken that the worms are not flooded with too much to eat.
 
• The bin should not be too dry or too wet. The moisture levels need to be checked periodically.
 
• They support the expansion of pests and pathogens such as fruit flies, centipede and flies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Illuviation:** It is the accumulation of dissolved or suspended soil materials in one area or layer as a result of leaching from another.
 
• **Leaching: **Leaching is the loss of soluble substances and colloids from the highest layer of soil by percolating precipitation.
 
• **Eluviation:** It is the removal of dissolved or suspended material from a layer or layers of the soil by the movement of water when rainfall exceeds evaporation.

__

question: Magnesium is present in which of the following?

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chlorophyll**

 
 
• Chlorophyll is the molecule that absorbs sunlight and uses its energy to synthesize carbohydrates from CO2 and water.
 
• This process is known as photosynthesis and is the basis for sustaining the life processes of all plants.
 
• Since animals and humans obtain their food supply by eating plants, photosynthesis can be said to be the source of our life also.
 
• Chlorophyll is the molecule that traps this 'most elusive of all powers' - and is called a photoreceptor.
 
• It is found in the chloroplasts of green plants and is what makes green plants, green.
 
• The basic structure of a chlorophyll molecule is a porphyrin ring, coordinated to a central atom.
 
• **This is very similar in structure to the heme group found in hemoglobin, except that in heme the central atom is iron, whereas in chlorophyll it is magnesium.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Hemoglobin (Hb) is a protein found in red blood cells that carries oxygen in your body and gives blood its red color.
 
• Hemoglobin levels vary from person to person.
 
• Men usually have higher levels than women.
 
• A hemoglobin “cut-off” level is set for blood donation to ensure that your hemoglobin will not drop below normal after you have donated blood.
 
• Normal ranges for hemoglobin differ between ethnic populations, and males and females, and are also affected by age, especially in women.
 
• Individuals with hemoglobin levels below the normal range are, by definition, anemic.
 
 
 
• **Cytochrome**
 
 
• Cytochrome participates in the production of ATP in the electron transport cycle in mitochondria.
 
• It helps in transferring electrons in ETC.
 
• Cytochrome c is released into the cytosol and triggers programmed cell death during apoptosis.
 
 
 
• **ATP stands for Adenosine Tri Phosphate**
 
 
• ATP are the main source of energy within the Cell
 
• It is produced by enzyme ATP synthase which Converts ADP and Phosphate to ATP
 
• It is a complex organic chemical that provides energy to drive many processes in a living cell. Eg.- muscle contraction, nerve impulse propagation, and chemical synthesis.

question: Which of the following is a group of chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and primarily aquatic (both freshwater and marine) organisms?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Algae**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Algae** are a diverse group of chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic organisms.
 
• They are primarily **aquatic**, found in both freshwater and marine environments.
 
• Algae are capable of **photosynthesis** and produce oxygen as a byproduct.
 
• They play a crucial role in aquatic ecosystems as **primary producers**.
 
• Algae can vary in size from microscopic **phytoplankton** to large seaweeds like kelp.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chlorophyll**

 
 
• Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria.
 
• It is essential for photosynthesis, allowing plants to absorb light energy from the sun.
 
• There are several types of chlorophyll, with chlorophyll-a being the most common in algae.
 
 
 
• **Thalloid**
 
 
• The term "thalloid" refers to the simple, undifferentiated body structure of certain plants and algae.
 
• Unlike higher plants, thalloid organisms do not have roots, stems, or leaves.
 
• Examples include liverworts and certain types of algae.
 
 
 
• **Photosynthesis**
 
 
• Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize foods with the help of chlorophyll.
 
• It involves the transformation of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
 
• This process is fundamental to the survival of life on Earth, providing the primary energy source for all living organisms.
 
 
 
• **Aquatic Ecosystems**
 
 
• Aquatic ecosystems include both freshwater and marine environments where algae are commonly found.
 
• These ecosystems are vital for the global carbon cycle and support a diverse range of organisms.
 
• Algae serve as the foundation of the food web in aquatic ecosystems.
 
 
 
• **Phytoplankton**
 
 
• Phytoplankton are microscopic algae that float in the water column of oceans and freshwater bodies.
 
• They are primary producers, forming the base of the aquatic food chain.

__
 
• **Ethylene** is a plant hormone that plays a key role in the **ripening of climacteric fruits**, such as bananas, tomatoes, and apples.
 
• It is the only gaseous plant hormone and is naturally produced by fruits during the ripening process.
 
• Ethylene promotes changes in color, texture, and flavor of fruits by influencing the breakdown of chlorophyll and the conversion of starches to sugars.
 
• It also regulates other processes like **flower senescence** and the shedding of leaves (abscission).
 
• Commercially, ethylene is used to **artificially induce ripening** in fruits post-harvest to meet market demands.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gibberellin:**

 
 
• Stimulates stem elongation, seed germination, and flowering.
 
• It plays a key role in breaking seed dormancy and promoting the growth of internodes in plants like sugarcane.
 
 
 
• **Cytokinin:**
 
 
• Primarily regulates **cell division** and promotes shoot growth.
 
• It also delays leaf senescence and works in conjunction with auxins for plant development.
 
 
 
• **Auxin:**
 
 
• Promotes cell elongation, root initiation, and apical dominance.
 
• Auxins are also involved in phototropism and gravitropism, helping plants respond to environmental stimuli.
 
 
 
• **Abscisic Acid (ABA):**
 
 
• Known as the "stress hormone," it regulates stomatal closure during water stress.
 
• ABA induces seed dormancy and is involved in leaf abscission.

question: In 1942, who presented the "Trophic-dynamic aspect of Ecology," which is the basic process of energy transfer from one trophic level to another in an ecosystem?
solution:
The correct answer is **Raymond L Lindeman**. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****Trophic-dynamic aspect of ecology:**

__
 
• The fundamental process by which energy moves from one trophic level to the next in an ecosystem is known as trophic dynamics.

**Energy flow in the ecosystem:**

 
• In a food chain, the energy flow follows the 10 per cent law.
 
• According to this law, only **10 per cent of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the other; the rest is lost into the atmosphere.**
 
• This energy is stored in various organic products in the plants from the sun via the process of photosynthesis.
 
• This is then** passed on to the primary consumers in the food chain when the herbivores consume (primary consumers) the plants as food.**
 
• Then conversion of chemical energy stored in plant products into kinetic energy occurs, degradation of energy will occur through its conversion into heat.
 
• **The energy flow is: Primary (100%) → First level/ Primary (10%) → Second-level/ Secondary (1%) → Third level / Tertiary (0.1%).**
 
• **The energy flow in the ecosystem is clearly unidirectional**.
 
• The** ten percent rule of transfer of energy** from one trophic level to the next is being credited to **Raymond Lindeman (1942).**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Arthur Tansley:**

 
• It was in **1935 that Arthur Tansley**, the British ecologist, **coined the term 'ecosystem'**.
 
• It is the **interactive system established between the biocoenosis (the group of living creatures), and their biotope**, the environment in which they live.

**Ernst Haeckel:**

 
• The word **“Ecology” was coined by “Ernst Haeckel”**.
 
• It is the branch of biology that studies organizations in their environment.
 
• Ecology word is taken from the** Greek word Oekologie, Oikos meaning “House” and logos meaning “Study”**.
 
• **Ecology is the study of the household**.
 
• Ernst Haeckel** also proposed the theory of development and evolution**.

**Charles Elton:**

 
• The **concept of the ecological pyramid was first proposed by Charles Elton in 1927.**
 
• It was known as the **Eltonian pyramid** then.** E.P. Odum wrote the popular ecology book 'Fundamentals of Ecology' in 1953**.

subject: GK
question: Identify a structure that plays a role in motility.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Flagella**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Flagella** are long, whip-like structures that protrude from the cell body of certain prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, aiding in cell motility.
 
• They are primarily composed of a protein called **flagellin** in prokaryotes and **microtubules** arranged in a 9+2 arrangement in eukaryotes.
 
• Flagella move in a propeller-like motion to propel the cell through its environment, essential for the locomotion of many bacteria and sperm cells.
 
• In bacteria, flagella can be located at one end of the cell (polar), both ends (amphitrichous), or all over the cell surface (peritrichous).
 
• The rotation of the flagella is powered by a motor protein complex located at the base of the flagellum, driven by the flow of protons across the cell membrane.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pili**

 
 
• Pili are short, hair-like structures on the surface of prokaryotic cells that are involved in attachment to surfaces and in conjugation (DNA transfer between cells).
 
• Pili are made of a protein called pilin and are not involved in motility.
 
 
 
• **Villi**
 
 
• Villi are small, finger-like projections found in the small intestine of many vertebrates.
 
• They increase the surface area for absorption of nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Fimbriae**
 
 
• Fimbriae are similar to pili but are typically more numerous and shorter.
 
• They are used by bacteria to adhere to host cells and surfaces, aiding in colonization and infection.
 
 
 
• **Cilia**
 
 
• Cilia are short, hair-like structures found on the surface of eukaryotic cells.
 
• They can move in a coordinated manner to move fluid or mucus over the cell surface or to propel single-celled organisms.

question: What is the vitamin deficiency in milk?
solution:
The correct answer is __**C**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Milk is a poor source of Vitamin C.
 
• Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, is essential for the repair of tissues and the enzymatic production of certain neurotransmitters.
 
• Human bodies cannot synthesize Vitamin C, thus it must be obtained from the diet.
 
• Common sources of Vitamin C include fruits like oranges, strawberries, kiwi, and vegetables like bell peppers and spinach.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vitamin C Deficiency (Scurvy)**

 
 
• Scurvy is a disease resulting from a deficiency of Vitamin C.
 
• Symptoms of scurvy include anemia, debility, exhaustion, spontaneous bleeding, pain in the limbs, and especially the legs, swelling in some parts of the body, and ulceration of the gums and loss of teeth.
 
• Scurvy can be prevented and treated with adequate intake of Vitamin C.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Vitamin C**
 
 
• Vitamin C is important for the biosynthesis of collagen, L-carnitine, and certain neurotransmitters.
 
• It is also involved in protein metabolism.
 
• Vitamin C is a potent antioxidant and helps in the regeneration of other antioxidants within the body.
 
 
 
• **Dietary Sources of Vitamin C**
 
 
• Citrus fruits like oranges, lemons, and grapefruits are rich sources of Vitamin C.
 
• Other fruits such as strawberries, kiwi, and guava also contain high levels of Vitamin C.
 
• Vegetables like bell peppers, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, and spinach are good sources of Vitamin C.
 
 
 
• **Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)**
 
 
• The RDA for Vitamin C varies by age, gender, and life stage.
 
• For example, adult men are recommended to consume 90 mg per day while adult women should consume 75 mg per day.
 
• Smokers are advised to consume an additional 35 mg per day due to the increased oxidative stress from smoking.

subject: GK
question: Who among the following was the first to describe the nucleus as a cell organelle?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Robert Brown**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Robert Brown was a Scottish botanist who made significant contributions to botany and plant morphology.
 
• He is credited with the discovery of the cell nucleus in 1831.
 
• Brown's observations were made while studying the cells of orchid plants.
 
• His work laid the foundation for the cell theory, which is fundamental to modern biology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cell Theory**

 
 
• Proposed by Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann in 1839.
 
• States that all living organisms are composed of cells and that the cell is the basic unit of life.
 
• Later expanded by Rudolf Virchow who stated that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
 
 
 
• **Robert Brown's Other Contributions**
 
 
• Described the phenomenon known as Brownian motion, the random movement of particles suspended in a fluid.
 
• Published significant works on plant pollination mechanisms and plant taxonomy.
 
 
 
• **Nucleus Function**
 
 
• The nucleus is the control center of the cell, housing the cell's genetic material (DNA).
 
• Responsible for regulating gene expression and mediating the replication of DNA during the cell cycle.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**
 
 
• Brown's discovery came during a period of rapid advances in microscopy and cell biology.
 
• The 19th century saw many foundational discoveries in biology that paved the way for modern science.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is not a correct statement regarding vacuoles?

options.text: Vacuoles are generally larger in animal cells than in plant cells.
Animal cells usually contain smaller vacuoles compared to plant cells
In some plant cells, the central vacuole can take up most of the cell's volume
Vacuoles serve as storage sacs for both solids and liquids

solution:
The correct answer is __**Vacuoles are generally larger in animal cells than in plant cells**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Vacuoles are significantly larger in plant cells compared to animal cells, where they typically occupy a central position and can take up most of the cell's volume.
 
• In animal cells, vacuoles are smaller and more numerous, often serving specialized functions like storage and waste disposal.
 
• Plant vacuoles are surrounded by a membrane called the tonoplast and play critical roles in maintaining turgor pressure, which supports the plant's structure.
 
• The primary function of vacuoles includes storage of nutrients and waste products, maintaining cell homeostasis, and isolating harmful substances.
 
• Option 1 is incorrect because vacuoles are larger in plant cells than animal cells, not the other way around.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Central Vacuole (Plant Cells):**

 
 
• It is a large vacuole found in most mature plant cells, surrounded by the tonoplast membrane.
 
• Functions include storage of water, nutrients, and waste products, as well as maintaining cell rigidity through turgor pressure.
 
 
 
• **Vacuoles in Animal Cells:**
 
 
• Animal cells usually have smaller vacuoles that perform specialized roles such as storage, transport, and waste management.
 
• They do not occupy a central position as in plant cells.
 
 
 
• **Tonoplast Membrane:**
 
 
• The tonoplast is a semi-permeable membrane surrounding the plant vacuole, regulating the movement of ions and molecules.
 
• It helps in maintaining the vacuole's internal environment and plays a role in osmoregulation.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Vacuoles:**
 
 
• Storage of nutrients, ions, and waste materials.
 
• Isolation of harmful substances and maintenance of internal hydrostatic pressure.
 
• Facilitating cellular processes such as autophagy and ion balance.

question: In which of the following conditions is there severe physical and mental retardation due to deficiency of iodine and thyroid hormones, especially during early pregnancy?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Cretinism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cretinism**:-

 
 
• **It is a severe form of iodine deficiency disorder (IDD) that can cause irreversible physical and mental retardation.**
 
• **Cretinism is most commonly caused by iodine deficiency during pregnancy and early infancy.**
 
• Iodine is a trace element that is essential for the production of thyroid hormones.
 
• Thyroid hormones are important for the normal development of the brain and nervous system.
 
• If a pregnant woman or a young child does not get enough iodine, it can lead to a deficiency of thyroid hormones, which can cause cretinism.
 
• Symptoms of cretinism can include:-
 
 
• Severe mental retardation
 
• Stunted growth
 
• Deafness
 
• Mutism
 
• Spasticity
 
• Goiter (enlarged thyroid gland)
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Preeclampsia**:-

 
 
• **It is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and protein in the urine after 20 weeks of pregnancy. **
 
• It can lead to serious health problems for both mother and baby, including seizures, liver and kidney damage, and premature birth.
 
 
 
• **Toxoplasmosis**:-
 
 
• **It is an infection caused by a parasite called Toxoplasma gondii. **
 
• It can be spread through contact with infected cats or their feces, contaminated meat, or unwashed fruits and vegetables.
 
• While most people who are infected with Toxoplasma gondii never experience any symptoms, it can cause serious birth defects if a woman is infected during pregnancy.
 
 
 
• **Syphilis**:-
 
 
• **It is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. **
 
• It can be spread through contact with open sores on the skin or mucous membranes.
 
• While syphilis can be cured with antibiotics, it can cause serious birth defects if a woman is infected during pregnancy.

• Rickets is a skeletal disorder that results from a deficiency of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate.
 
• It leads to softening and weakening of the bones in children, potentially causing bone deformities.
 
• Common symptoms include delayed growth, pain in the spine, pelvis, and legs, and muscle weakness.
 
• Rickets can lead to skeletal deformities such as bowed legs or thickened wrists and ankles.
 
• The disease can be prevented by ensuring adequate intake of vitamin D, calcium, and phosphate through diet and sunlight exposure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vitamin D**

 
 
• Vitamin D is crucial for the absorption of calcium and phosphate in the body.
 
• It can be obtained through dietary sources such as fatty fish, fortified dairy products, and supplements.
 
• Sunlight exposure also triggers vitamin D synthesis in the skin.
 
 
 
• **Calcium**
 
 
• Calcium is essential for the development and maintenance of strong bones and teeth.
 
• Dairy products, leafy green vegetables, and fortified foods are good sources of calcium.
 
 
 
• **Phosphate**
 
 
• Phosphate plays a key role in bone formation and energy storage and release.
 
• It is found in foods such as meat, fish, dairy products, and whole grains.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Treatment**
 
 
• Ensuring a balanced diet with adequate vitamin D, calcium, and phosphate is crucial for preventing rickets.
 
• Supplementation may be necessary in cases of deficiency or limited sun exposure.
 
• Medical treatment for rickets may include high doses of vitamin D and calcium supplements.
 
• In severe cases, corrective surgery may be required for bone deformities.

question: Identify a hydrocarbon pair that is NOT the part of the homologous series.
solution:
The correct answer is C4H4 and C5H10__**.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **A series of hydrocarbons** having **similar chemical properties** and **sharing the same general formula** constitute a **homologous series**. 
 
• Each member of a homologous series differs from the succeeding or preceding member by CH2.
 
• These organic compounds** have a similar structure and functional group**.
 
• The hydrocarbons in a homologous series **show a gradation in physical properties**.
 
• For example- CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈,... represent the homologous series of **alkanes** having general formula as **CₙH****₂ₙ₊₂****, **where n denotes the number of carbon atoms**. **Successive terms of the series differ by CH₂.
 
• Similarly, C₂H4, C3H6, C4H8,... represent the homologous series of **alkenes** having general formula as **CnH****2n**. Here also, the successive terms differ by CH2.
 
• Also, C₂H₂, C₃H₄, C₄H₆,... represent the homologous series of **alkynes **having general formula as **CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. **Again the successive terms differ by CH2.
 
• Clearly, **C2H6 and C3H9 are not part of the homologous series as they do not differ by the molecular formula of CH****2** but differ by CH3.​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Characteristics of Homologous Series**

 
 
• **​**All members of a homologous series can be **represented by a** **general formula**.
 
• Each member of a homologous series **differs** **from its successive or preceding member** **by the molecular formula of CH****2**.
 
• Each member of a homologous series **differs from its successive or preceding member by the molecular mass of 14**.
 
• All members of a homologous series can be** prepared by the same general method**.
 
• All members of a homologous series have the** same chemical properties** due to the presence of the same functional group.
 
• Due to different molecular masses, members of a homologous series **show differences in physical properties** like melting point, boiling point, solubility, etc.** but with a gradation**.

__
 
• **Picric acid**, also called **2,4,6-trinitrophenol,** pale yellow, odourless crystalline solid that has been used as a **military explosive,** as a **yellow dye**, and as an **antiseptic**. 
 
• Picric acid can be described as an organic compound whose formula is **(O₂N)₃C₆H₂OH** and the IUPAC name of this acid is 3C₆ **2,4,6-trinitrophenol (TNP)**. Due to its bitter taste, the name **"picric"** comes from the Greek word (pikros), which means "bitter."

• Beginning in 1849, it was employed as a yellow dye, initially for silk.
 
• Picric acid was once highly valuable as an **explosive** and was first used as a bursting charge for shells by the French in 1886, under the name melinite.
 
• Picric acid was the most extensively utilized **military explosive** by the time of the Russo-Japanese War.
 
• Its very corrosive action on the metal surfaces of shells, on the other hand, was a drawback, and its use dropped after World War I.

 A process that affects the form of a chemical substance, but not its chemical composition. Examples include changes in state or temperature.

question: When do the drugs used as medicines become potential poisons?

options.text: When doses are taken as recommended
When doses are taken at the recommended time and in the recommended quantity
When doses are taken higher than recommended
When doses are taken lower than recommended

solution:
The correct answer is __**When doses are taken higher than recommended**__. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Medicines become potential poisons** when dosages exceed the levels deemed safe and effective by medical guidelines.
 
• Overdosing can lead to **toxic effects** which may cause severe organ damage or even be **fatal**.
 
• It is crucial to follow the prescribed amount and frequency to avoid adverse effects and ensure the drug's efficacy and safety.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Therapeutic Window: **

 
 
• Drugs have a **therapeutic window** which is the range between the minimum effective dose and the toxic dose.
 
• Staying within this window is crucial for the safe use of any medication.
 
 
 
• **Monitoring and Adjustments: **
 
 
• Regular monitoring of drug levels may be necessary, especially for medications with a narrow therapeutic window.
 
• Dose adjustments based on individual responses and interactions with other medications are vital for maintaining safety.
 
 
 
• **Risk Awareness:**
 
 
• Patients and caregivers should be educated about the risks of overdose and the importance of adhering to prescribed dosages.

question: By whom was the equation C = KPgₐₛ formulated in 1803?
solution:
The correct answer is __**William Henry.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** C = KPgₐₛ**

 
 
• **​The equation C = KPgₐₛ, also known as Henry's Law, was formulated by William Henry, an English chemist and physician, in 1803.**
 
• This law states that the amount of a gas that dissolves in a given type and volume of liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas in equilibrium with that liquid.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Edme Mariotte:-**

 
 
• **He was a French physicist and priest who is best known for his work on the relationship between the pressure and volume of gases. **
 
• In 1679, he published a paper in which he stated that the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume at a constant temperature.
 
• This is known as Boyle's Law, after Robert Boyle, who had independently discovered the same relationship in 1662.
 
 
 
• **Jacques Charles:-**
 
 
• **He was a French physicist and mathematician who is best known for his work on the relationship between the volume and temperature of gases. **
 
• In 1787, he published a paper in which he stated that the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature at a constant pressure. This is known as Charles's Law.
 
 
 
• **Robert Boyle:-**
 
 
• **He was an English natural philosopher, chemist, physicist, inventor, alchemist, and theologian. **
 
• Boyle is best known for his formulation of the Boyle–Mariotte law, an experimental relationship between the volume and pressure of a gas at a constant temperature.
 
• His work in chemistry included the discovery of hydrogen and the formulation of the gas laws. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern chemistry.

question: In acetylene (C₂H₂), hybridzation of carbon atoms is:
solution:
The correct answer is __**sp**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In acetylene (C2H2),** the hybridization of carbon atoms is sp. **
 
• In acetylene, the carbon atoms are connected by a **triple bond**, consisting of **one sigma bond** and **two pi bonds**.
 
• To form the linear structure of acetylene and accommodate the triple bond, each carbon atom undergoes **sp hybridization**.
 
• The sp hybridization involves mixing one s orbital and one p orbital, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals that form the two pi bonds.
 
• The bond angle in sp hybridization is **180°**, giving acetylene its linear shape.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hybridizatio**n is the process of combining carbon atom's atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals.
 
• These hybrid orbitals have** different shapes and energies than the original orbitals.** 
 
• **Benefits of hybridization**
 
 
• Hybridization allows carbon to form strong sigma bonds, which contributes to the structural integrity of organic compounds. 
 
• Hybridization gives carbon the flexibility to form a variety of geometries and chemical and physical properties.

question: What is the name of the solution that is employed to identify the existence of starch in food?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Iodine solution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Iodine solution is used to test for the presence of starch in food items.
 
• When iodine solution is added to a sample containing starch, the solution changes its color to blue-black.
 
• This color change is due to the formation of a starch-iodine complex.
 
• The test is simple and widely used in both educational and laboratory settings.
 
• It is a qualitative test, indicating the presence or absence of starch rather than measuring the amount.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Starch**

 
 
• Starch is a carbohydrate consisting of a large number of glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds.
 
• It is produced by most green plants as an energy store.
 
• Common sources of starch include potatoes, rice, and wheat.
 
• In the human diet, starch is a major source of energy.
 
 
 
• **Iodine Solution**
 
 
• Iodine solution, also known as Lugol's iodine, consists of iodine and potassium iodide dissolved in water.
 
• It is commonly used in medical and biological applications.
 
• Besides testing for starch, it is used as a disinfectant and antiseptic.
 
 
 
• **Starch-Iodine Complex**
 
 
• The blue-black color observed in the test is due to the formation of a starch-iodine complex.
 
• This complex forms when iodine molecules fit inside the helical structure of the amylose component of starch.
 
• The exact nature of this complex is still a subject of research, but it is believed that the iodine gets trapped in the helical structure, leading to the color change.
 
 
 
• **Other Tests for Carbohydrates**
 
 
• Benedict's test is used to identify reducing sugars.
 
• Fehling's test also identifies reducing sugars.
 
• Barfoed's test differentiates between monosaccharides and disaccharides.
 
• Each test has a specific reagent and mechanism for detecting different types of carbohydrates.

question: What is the boiling point of water at sea level?
solution:
The Correct answer is __**212 ºF**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **boiling point of water** at sea level is **212 ºF**, which is equivalent to **100 ºC**.
 
• This boiling point is determined under **standard atmospheric pressure**, which is approximately **1 atmosphere (101.325 kPa).**
 
• At this temperature, water transitions from the **liquid phase to the gas phase**, forming steam.
 
• The boiling point of water can change with variations in **altitude and atmospheric pressure.** For example, at higher altitudes, where the atmospheric pressure is lower, water boils at a temperature **below 212 ºF.**
 
• Boiling water is crucial in various **scientific, industrial, and daily applications,** such as cooking, sterilization, and generating steam for energy production.
 
• The boiling point of water is often used as a reference point in **thermometry** and other scientific measurements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Altitude and Boiling Point Relationship**__

 __
 
• As altitude increases, the **atmospheric pressure decreases**, which reduces the boiling point of water.
 
• For example, at an altitude of around **5,000 feet**, water boils at approximately **203 ºF.**
 
• This principle is significant in **mountainous regions** and affects cooking times for food preparation.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Boiling Water**__
 
 
• Boiling water is widely used for **purification** and sterilization to kill harmful microbes.
 
• It is a key component in **steam engines**, which were historically significant in industrial development.
 
• Boiling water plays an essential role in **scientific experiments** and chemical processes.

question: What is the term used to refer to the process of conversion of water vapour back to water?
solution:
__
 
• **Condensation**__ is the process of conversion of water vapour back to the water.
 
• Condensation is the change of the physical state of matter from the gas phase into the liquid phase and is the reverse of vaporization.
 
• Condensation is initiated by the formation of atomic/molecular clusters of that species within its gaseous volume—like a raindrop or snowflake formation within clouds—or at the contact between such gaseous phase and a liquid or solid surface.
 
• Vapour cooling and compressing equipment that collects condensed liquids is called a "condenser".
 
• Evaporation is a type of vaporization that occurs on the surface of a liquid as it changes into the gas phase.
 
• Freezing is a phase transition where a liquid turns into a solid when its temperature is lowered below its freezing point.
 
• Sublimation is the transition of a substance directly from the solid to the gas phase, without passing through the intermediate liquid phase.

question: The heat energy absorbed or released at constant temperature per unit mass for change of state is called by what name?
solution:
__
 
• The heat energy absorbed or released at constant temperature per unit mass for change of state is called **latent heat**__.
 
• When it is associated with freezing a liquid or melting a solid, then that is known as the heat of fusion.
 
• The one associated with condensing a vapour or vaporizing a solid or liquid is known as the heat of vaporization.

 
 

 
 
SUBLIMATION

 
 
 
Sublimation is the transition of a substance directly from the solid to the gas phase without undergoing the intermediate liquid phase. The converse is known as desublimation or deposition where substances convert directly from the gaseous state to a solid without first undergoing a liquid state.

 
 
 

 
 
LIQUEFACTION

 
 
 
Liquefaction of gases is the process by which substances in their gaseous state are converted to the liquid state

 
 
 

 
 
LATENT HEAT OF FUSION

 
 
 
Amount of heat energy that is required to change 1 Kg of a solid into liquid at atmospheric pressure at its melting point

 
 
 

 
 
LATENT HEAT OF VAPORIZATION

 
 
 
The heat absorbed per unit mass of a given material at its boiling point that completely converts the material to a gas at the same temperature

• **Charles's Law** for a** fixed mass of a gas** at constant pressure, **volume of a gas increases on increasing temperature and decreases on cooling**

question: Which is a beta-emitting radioactive isotope of hydrogen that has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus, making it three times as heavy as a hydrogen nucleus and one and a half times heavier than deuterium?

• It is a beta-emitting radioactive isotope of hydrogen.
 
• Its nucleus consists of one proton and two neutrons, making it three times as heavy as a hydrogen nucleus (with its one proton) and one-and-a-half times as heavy as deuterium (which contains one proton and only one neutron).
 
• Tritium would no longer exist in our environment if cosmic radiation produces it in the atmosphere in very small amounts.
 
• The half-life of the unstable tritium nucleus is of 12.3 years, which is very short on the radioactive time scale.

 Protium
 
 
 
• **Protium **has no neutrons in its nucleus.
 
• It is considered the most stable isotope of hydrogen.
 
• The basic hydrogen atom – a single proton circled by a single electron is also called protium.
 
 
 
 

 Hydrogen-4
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen-4** is a **highly unstable isotope of hydrogen.**
 
• The nucleus consists of **a proton** and **three neutrons**.

 Calcium (Ca) is another alkaline earth metal, essential for living organisms, especially in bone formation.

question: Which process of phase transition is the reverse of deposition?
solution:
The correct answer is **__Sublimation__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Sublimation is the transition of a substance directly from the solid to the gas phase without passing through the intermediate liquid phase.
 
• Deposition, on the other hand, is the reverse process where a gas transforms directly into a solid without becoming a liquid first.
 
• This makes sublimation the reverse of deposition as it involves a direct solid to gas transition.
 
• Both processes are phase transitions that occur under specific temperature and pressure conditions.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
 

 Option
 Details
 
 

 1) Sublimation
 Direct transition from solid to gas.
 
 

 2) Fusion
 Melting, or the process where a solid turns into a liquid.
 
 

 3) Solidification
 Freezing, or the process where a liquid turns into a solid.
 
 

 4) Vaporisation
 The phase transition from liquid to gas.

question: What was the symbol Henry Moseley used for denoting atomic number?
solution:
The correct answer is **__Z__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Henry Moseley discovered that the atomic number of an element is a more fundamental property than its atomic mass.
 
• Moseley used the symbol Z to denote the atomic number, which represents the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.
 
• This discovery led to the reorganization of the periodic table based on atomic numbers rather than atomic masses.
 
• Moseley's work provided the foundation for the modern periodic law, which states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Henry Moseley was an English physicist who made significant contributions to the understanding of atomic structure.
 
• His experiments with X-ray spectra allowed him to determine the charge on the nucleus of atoms, leading to the accurate determination of atomic numbers.
 
• Moseley's law mathematically related the frequency of X-rays emitted by an element to its atomic number.
 
• Tragically, Moseley was killed in World War I, cutting short a brilliant scientific career that had already had a profound impact on chemistry and physics.

• In 1866, **John Newlands, an English scientist, **arranged the then-known elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
 
• He started with the element with the lowest atomic mass (hydrogen) and ended with **Thorium** which was the** 56th element.**
 
• He found that every eighth element has the same properties as the first. He compared it to the octave found in music.

• The properties of lithium and sodium were found to be similar in Newlands' octave.

• But, later on, several new elements were discovered, whose properties did not fit into the Law of Octaves.
 
• In **1869**, just five years after **John Newlands **put forward his Law of Octaves, a Russian chemist called **Dmitri Mendeleev published a periodic table.**
 
• **Mendeleev** also arranged the elements known at the time in order of **relative atomic mass**, but he did some other things that made his table much more successful.
 
• **Marie Curie **is best remembered for discovering radium and polonium, and for her huge contribution to finding treatments for cancer.

question: Identify the correct statement related to metallic character.

options.text: Metallic character stays the same across a period and decreases the same down a group.
Metallic character decreases across a group and stays the same down a group.
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Metallic character increases across a period and decreases down a group.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Metallic character** refers to the level of reactivity of a metal.
 
• Across a period from left to right, **metallic character decreases** because elements become less willing to lose electrons.
 
• Down a group, the **metallic character increases** due to the increase in atomic size, which makes it easier for atoms to lose electrons.
 
• Elements on the left side of the periodic table (alkali metals) have the highest metallic character, whereas elements on the right side (noble gases) have the least.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ionization Energy:** The energy required to remove an electron from an atom. It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
 
• **Electronegativity:** The ability of an atom to attract electrons. It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
 
• **Atomic Radius:** The size of an atom. It decreases across a period and increases down a group.
 
• **Non-metallic Character:** Opposite of metallic character, it increases across a period and decreases down a group.
 
• **Periodic Trends:** Understanding these trends helps in predicting the chemical behavior of elements.

question: Which of the following has the highest density?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Solid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Solids have the highest density compared to liquids, gases, and plasma because their particles are packed closely together in a fixed structure.
 
• The density of a material is defined as its mass per unit volume. Solids generally exhibit the highest mass per unit volume among the states of matter.
 
• Examples of high-density solids include metals such as iron, gold, and lead, which have densities significantly higher than liquids and gases.
 
• Solids retain a fixed shape and volume, contributing to their higher density, whereas liquids and gases conform to the shape of their containers and have lower densities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Density**

 
 
• Density is a measure of how much mass is contained in a given unit volume of a substance.
 
• The formula for density is: Density = Mass / Volume.
 
 
 
• **States of Matter**
 
 
• There are four fundamental states of matter: solid, liquid, gas, and plasma.
 
• Each state has distinct physical properties, such as shape, volume, and particle arrangement.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Densities**
 
 
• Solids typically have the highest densities, followed by liquids, gases, and then plasma.
 
• Water has a density of approximately 1 g/cm³ at standard temperature and pressure, while air has a density of about 0.0012 g/cm³.
 
 
 
• **Plasma**
 
 
• Plasma is a high-energy state of matter where electrons are stripped from atoms, creating a mixture of positively charged ions and free electrons.
 
• Plasma densities are typically lower than those of solids, liquids, and gases under terrestrial conditions.

question: Who introduced the term 'triads' in the classification of elements?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Johann Dobereiner**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Johann Dobereiner, a German chemist, introduced the concept of 'triads' in 1817.
 
• He observed that certain groups of three elements (triads) had similar chemical properties and that the atomic weight of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two.
 
• Dobereiner's Triads were an early attempt to classify elements based on their properties and paved the way for the development of the periodic table.
 
• Examples of Dobereiner's Triads include lithium, sodium, and potassium, as well as calcium, strontium, and barium.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Periodic Table Development:**

 
 
• The periodic table as we know it today was developed by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869.
 
• Mendeleev arranged elements in order of increasing atomic weight and left gaps for elements that were yet to be discovered.
 
 
 
• **Law of Triads:**
 
 
• The Law of Triads states that the arithmetic mean of the atomic weights of the first and third elements in a triad is approximately equal to the atomic weight of the second element.
 
 
 
• **Other Early Classifications:**
 
 
• John Newlands proposed the Law of Octaves, which stated that every eighth element had similar properties.
 
• A.E.B. de Chancourtois introduced the telluric helix, a three-dimensional arrangement of the elements.
 
 
 
• **Modern Periodic Law:**
 
 
• The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers, not atomic weights.
 
• This law was proposed by Henry Moseley in 1913 after he discovered the concept of atomic number.

__
 
• **Lithium** is an element that does not belong to period 4 of the periodic table.
 
• Lithium is placed in **period 2** of the periodic table and is part of the alkali metals group.
 
• Elements like **Calcium, Zinc, and Potassium** are all found in period 4 of the periodic table.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Periodic Table**

 
 
• The periodic table is a tabular arrangement of chemical elements, organized by their atomic number, electron configuration, and recurring chemical properties.
 
• Elements are presented in order of increasing atomic number in rows called periods and columns called groups.
 
• The table provides a framework for analyzing chemical behavior and is widely used in chemistry and other sciences.
 
 
 
• **Period 4 Elements**
 
 
• Period 4 elements include Potassium (K), Calcium (Ca), Scandium (Sc), Titanium (Ti), Vanadium (V), Chromium (Cr), Manganese (Mn), Iron (Fe), Cobalt (Co), Nickel (Ni), Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Gallium (Ga), Germanium (Ge), Arsenic (As), Selenium (Se), Bromine (Br), and Krypton (Kr).
 
• These elements have their outermost electrons in the fourth shell.
 
 
 
• **Alkali Metals**
 
 
• Alkali metals are found in group 1 of the periodic table and include Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), Rubidium (Rb), Cesium (Cs), and Francium (Fr).
 
• They are highly reactive, especially with water, and are characterized by having one electron in their outermost shell.
 
 
 
• **Electronic Configuration**
 
 
• The electronic configuration of an element describes the distribution of electrons in its atomic orbitals.
 
• The configuration follows the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule, and the Pauli exclusion principle.
 
• For example, the electronic configuration of Lithium is 1s² 2s¹.

question: Which of Rutherford's experimental observations led him to conclude that the positive charge of an atom is concentrated in a very small region?

options.text: Electrons were found to orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels.
A very small fraction of a-particles rebounded almost backwards.
Most a-particles followed a straight path through the gold foil.
A small fraction of α-particles were deflected by small angles.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A very small fraction of α-particles rebounded almost backwards.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Rutherford's gold foil experiment involved the bombardment of a thin gold foil with α-particles (helium nuclei) to study atomic structure.
 
• Most α-particles passed through the foil undeflected, indicating that atoms are mostly empty space.
 
• A small fraction of α-particles were deflected at small angles, suggesting the presence of a positively charged center.
 
• A very tiny fraction of α-particles rebounded almost directly backward, leading Rutherford to conclude that the positive charge of the atom is concentrated in a very small, dense region, which he termed the nucleus.
 
• This observation provided experimental evidence for the nuclear model of the atom, replacing the earlier plum pudding model proposed by J.J. Thomson.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gold Foil Experiment:** Conducted in 1909 by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under the supervision of Ernest Rutherford, this experiment was pivotal in understanding atomic structure.
 
• **Nuclear Model of the Atom:** Proposed by Rutherford, it describes the atom as having a dense central nucleus containing protons, with electrons orbiting in the empty space surrounding it.
 
• **Plum Pudding Model:** An earlier atomic model proposed by J.J. Thomson, which suggested that electrons were embedded in a positively charged "pudding-like" substance. This model was disproved by Rutherford's experiment.
 
• **α-Particles:** Positively charged particles consisting of two protons and two neutrons, used as projectiles in the gold foil experiment.
 
• **Implications of Rutherford's Findings:** The discovery of the nucleus laid the foundation for the development of the modern quantum mechanical model of the atom and further studies on subatomic particles.

question: Which detergents are also used in toothpaste?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Anionic detergents**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Anionic detergents are commonly used in **toothpaste due to their effective cleansing properties.**
 
• **Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS)** is a prevalent anionic detergent found in many toothpaste formulations.
 
• Anionic detergents help in creating foam, which aids in the mechanical removal of food particles and plaque.
 
• These detergents are also responsible for the dispersion of ingredients in toothpaste, ensuring a uniform mixture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Surfactants:**

 
 
• Surfactants are compounds that lower the surface tension between two substances, such as a solid and a liquid.
 
• They are a key ingredient in many cleaning products, including toothpaste, detergents, and shampoos.
 
• Anionic surfactants, like sodium lauryl sulfate, are particularly effective in removing dirt and oil.
 
 
 
• **Sodium Lauryl Sulfate (SLS):**
 
 
• SLS is one of the most commonly used surfactants in toothpaste and other personal care products.
 
• It is known for its ability to produce a rich lather, which helps in the thorough cleaning of teeth.
 
• Despite its effectiveness, SLS can cause irritation in some individuals, leading to the development of alternative formulations.
 
 
 
• **Toothpaste Ingredients:**
 
 
• Common ingredients in toothpaste include abrasives, fluoride, flavoring agents, and humectants.
 
• Abrasives help in removing plaque and stains from the teeth, while fluoride strengthens tooth enamel.
 
• Humectants prevent the toothpaste from drying out, ensuring it remains usable over time.
 
 
 
• **Non-Ionic Detergents:**
 
 
• Non-ionic detergents are another class of surfactants that do not carry any charge.
 
• They are less likely to cause irritation and are often used in products designed for sensitive skin.
 
• While effective in cleaning, they are not as commonly used in toothpaste as anionic detergents.

question: What food items are most commonly affected by the adulteration of Sudan dyes?

The correct answer is __**Hot paprika**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Hot paprika is often subject to adulteration with Sudan dyes, which are industrial dyes that are not approved for use in food.
 
• Sudan dyes are used to enhance the color of hot paprika, making it appear more vibrant and appealing to consumers.
 
• The presence of Sudan dyes in food products is a significant health risk because they are known to be carcinogenic (cancer-causing).
 
• Regulatory agencies, such as the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), have strict regulations and testing procedures in place to detect and prevent the use of Sudan dyes in food products.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sudan Dyes**

 
 
• Sudan dyes are synthetic chemical dyes used in industrial applications for coloring oils, waxes, and polishes.
 
• They are not permitted in food products due to their potential health hazards, including being classified as carcinogens.
 
• Common types of Sudan dyes include Sudan I, II, III, and IV.
 
• Detection methods for Sudan dyes in food include high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and mass spectrometry.
 
 
 
• **Food Adulteration**
 
 
• Food adulteration is the act of intentionally degrading the quality of food by adding or removing substances.
 
• Adulteration can lead to serious health risks, including foodborne illnesses and long-term health effects.
 
• Common adulterants in spices include artificial colors, starch, and other cheaper substitutes.
 
• Regulatory bodies worldwide are continually updating guidelines and conducting inspections to prevent food adulteration.
 
 
 
• **Regulatory Agencies**
 
 
• Agencies such as the EFSA, FDA, and FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) are responsible for ensuring food safety.
 
• These agencies set maximum residue limits for contaminants and enforce food safety standards.
 
• They conduct regular inspections, testing, and certification to ensure compliance with food safety regulations.
 
• Public awareness campaigns are often conducted by these agencies to educate consumers about food safety and the risks of food adulteration.

subject: GK
question:
Match the column:

 
 

 
 
column A

 
(Conductor Type)

 
 
 
Column B

 
(Mobile Charge Carriers )

 
 
 

 
 
A.

 
 Metal
 
 
1.

 
 Positive and negative ions
 
 

 
 
B.

 
 lonised gas
 
 
2.

 
 Electrons and positively charged ions
 
 

 
 
C.

 
 Electrolyte
 
 
3.

 
 Electrons
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1) A - 3, B - 2, C - 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Metals** conduct electricity through **free electrons**, which move under the influence of an electric field, making them good conductors.
 
• An **ionised gas (plasma)** conducts via **electrons and positively charged ions**, as both species act as mobile charge carriers.
 
• **Electrolytes** such as acids, bases, and salts conduct current by movement of **positive (cations) and negative (anions)** ions in solution.
 
• This classification shows how different materials rely on different **mobile charge carriers** for conduction: electrons, ions, or both.
 
• The correct mapping is: **A–3 (Metal–Electrons), B–2 (Ionised gas–Electrons & Positive Ions), C–1 (Electrolyte–Positive & Negative Ions)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Conduction in Metals**

 
 
• Follows the **electron sea model**, where delocalised electrons move freely.
 
• Examples: copper, silver, and aluminium—excellent conductors due to high electron density.
 
 
 
• **Conduction in Ionised Gas (Plasma)**
 
 
• Plasma is called the **fourth state of matter**.
 
• Electricity conduction occurs due to **free electrons and ions** created by ionisation.
 
• Examples: fluorescent lamps, auroras, lightning.
 
 
 
• **Conduction in Electrolytes**
 
 
• Electrolytes dissociate into **ions in solution** (e.g., NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻).
 
• Used in **batteries, electrolysis, and biological systems**.
 
 
 
• **Key Concept**
 
 
• The type of **mobile charge carrier** determines the mechanism of current flow.
 
• Solids (metals) → electrons, Liquids (electrolytes) → ions, Gases (plasma) → ions + electrons.

question: Which of the following simple household methods can detect the presence of chalk powder in adulterated wheat flour?

options.text: Mixing with vinegar to observe fizzing reaction
Adding iodine solution to observe color change
Heating over flame to detect odor
Soaking in alcohol to dissolve the chalk

solution:
The correct answer is __**Mixing with vinegar to observe fizzing reaction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Chalk powder, primarily composed of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), reacts with acids like vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas.
 
• When vinegar is added to adulterated wheat flour containing chalk powder, fizzing or effervescence is observed due to the release of CO₂ gas.
 
• This simple household method is an effective and quick way to detect the presence of chalk powder in wheat flour.
 
• The reaction involved is: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑.
 
• Effervescence or bubbling confirms the presence of calcium carbonate in the adulterated wheat flour.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Adulteration:** It refers to the practice of adding unwanted substances to food items to increase quantity or reduce production costs, often compromising quality and safety.
 
• **Calcium Carbonate:** A common compound found in chalk, marble, and limestone. It is harmless in small amounts but is considered an adulterant when added to food products like flour.
 
• **Vinegar:** A household acid (acetic acid, CH₃COOH) commonly used in cooking and cleaning, making it a practical tool for such tests.
 
• **Effervescence:** The bubbling or fizzing that occurs due to the release of gas during a chemical reaction, such as the reaction of acids with carbonates.
 
• **Food Safety:** Regular checks for adulterants in food products are crucial to ensuring health and preventing long-term health risks associated with contaminated food.

question: In the context of cell organelles, a centriole is:

options.text: a stack of small flat sacs formed by membranes inside the cell's cytoplasm
a heterogeneous family of organelles found ubiquitously in plant cells
a paired barrel-shaped organelle located in the cytoplasm of animal cells near the nuclear envelope
a membrane-bound cell organelle that contains digestive enzymes

solution:
The correct answer is a __**paired barrel-shaped organelle located in the cytoplasm of animal cells near the nuclear envelope**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A centriole is a** barrel-shaped organelle found in animal cells, **
 
• **It p**rimarily responsible for **organizing microtubu**les and playing a crucial role in cell division by forming the poles of the mitotic spindle
 
• It is typically located near the** nucleus within a structure called the centrosome. **
 
• **It is **Composed of **nine sets of microtubule triplets** arranged in a cylindrical pattern. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• In the context of **cell biology, an "organelle" r**efers to a specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function, essentially acting like a tiny organ within the cell, with examples including the nucleus (which stores DNA), mitochondria (which produce energy), and the endoplasmic reticulum (involved in protein synthesis). 
 
• Each **organelle has a dedicated task to contribute to th**e overall function of the cell, similar to how organs in a body have specific roles. 
 
• **Examples of organelles:**
 
 
• **Nucleus:** Stores genetic material (DNA) and controls cellular activities. 
 
• **Mitochondria: "**Powerhouse of the cell," produces energy in the form of ATP. 
 
• **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)**: A network of membranes involved in protein synthesis and lipid production. 
 
• **Golgi apparatus**: Modifies and packages proteins for transport within the cell. 
 
• **Lysosomes**: Contain enzymes to break down waste materials. 
 
• **Ribosomes: **Small structures responsible for protein synthesis.

question: Identify a structure found in the form of vesicles, tubules and lamellae.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mesosomes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mesosomes are invaginated structures found in prokaryotic cells, particularly in bacteria.
 
• They appear in the form of vesicles, tubules, and lamellae within the bacterial cell.
 
• Mesosomes are involved in various cellular processes such as cell wall formation during cell division, DNA replication, and distribution to daughter cells.
 
• These structures are also associated with increasing the surface area of the plasma membrane for enzymatic activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Plastids**

 
 
• Plastids are double-membrane organelles found in the cells of plants and algae.
 
• They are involved in the synthesis and storage of food, most notably photosynthesis in chloroplasts.
 
 
 
• **Cytoplasm**
 
 
• The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance within the cell membrane, excluding the nucleus.
 
• It houses various organelles and is the site for most cellular processes.
 
 
 
• **Lysosomes**
 
 
• Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes.
 
• They break down waste materials and cellular debris.
 
 
 
• **Mesosomes in Detail**
 
 
• Mesosomes were once thought to be artifacts of cell preparation but are now considered functional structures.
 
• They play a role in the respiratory processes of the cell by hosting enzymes involved in cellular respiration.
